activist: A person who works hard, often in public, to change something they think is unfair, for example by organising protests or campaigns.
amendment: A change or addition to the Constitution of the United States. There have been 27 amendments since 1789.
american revolution: The war and the great change, from 1775 to 1783, through which the thirteen colonies freed themselves from Britain and became the United States.
armistice: An agreement to stop fighting in a war. It is not yet peace, but the guns fall silent.
artificial intelligence: Computer programs that can do things that seem to need human intelligence, like understanding language, recognising images or answering questions.
assembly line: A way of building things in a factory: the object moves slowly past a row of workers, and each one always does the same small task.
atomic bomb: An extremely powerful bomb that uses the energy inside atoms. One bomb can destroy a whole city. It has been used in war only twice, in 1945.
boycott: Refusing, all together, to buy something or use a service, as a peaceful protest to make a company or government change.
buffalo: The American bison, a huge wild animal with a hump and thick fur. About 30 million once lived on the Great Plains.
capitalist: In a capitalist economy, companies and businesses belong to private people, who sell goods freely and try to make a profit.
civil rights: The rights that every citizen should have equally: to vote, to go to school, to be treated fairly by the law, whatever their skin colour or origin.
climate change: The warming of the Earth caused mostly by the gases released when we burn oil, gas and coal. It brings more heatwaves, droughts, storms and floods.
colony: A territory far away that is ruled by another country. Its settlers are called colonists.
columbian exchange: The great exchange of plants, animals, foods, people and diseases between the Americas and the rest of the world after 1492.
communist: In a communist system, the state owns and controls factories, land and businesses. In the Soviet Union, one party ruled and people had few freedoms.
constitution: The most important law of a country. It says how the country is governed, who holds power, and what rights the citizens have.
continental congress: The meeting of representatives of the thirteen colonies, in Philadelphia, which led the fight against Britain and declared independence.
covered wagon: A wooden cart with a round white canvas roof, pulled by oxen, mules or horses. Pioneers carried all their belongings in it.
discrimination: Treating someone unfairly because of their skin colour, origin, religion, sex or something else they cannot change.
electricity: A form of energy made by tiny particles called electrons. Lightning is a giant electric spark. Today, electricity powers lights and machines.
empire: A very large state, often made up of many peoples and lands, ruled by one country or one ruler.
epidemic: When a disease spreads quickly and makes many people ill at the same time.
federal: In a federal country, power is shared between a national government and the governments of the states.
firefighter: A person whose job is to put out fires and rescue people in danger.
first lady: The title given to the wife of the President of the United States.
founding father: The Founding Fathers are the leaders who created the United States, such as George Washington, Benjamin Franklin, Thomas Jefferson and John Adams.
geyser: A hot spring that shoots boiling water and steam high into the air, from time to time.
health insurance: A system where people pay a little money regularly so that their doctor and hospital bills are paid when they are ill.
hiawatha: According to Haudenosaunee tradition, a leader who helped the Peacemaker unite the five nations. He is not the same as the hero of a famous poem by Longfellow.
hunger strike: Refusing to eat, as a protest, to draw attention to an injustice.
hunter-gatherer: A person who lives by hunting animals, fishing and gathering wild plants, fruits and roots, moving around instead of farming.
ice age: A long period when the Earth was much colder than today and huge sheets of ice covered the north of the continents.
immigrant: A person who comes to live in a new country.
improvisation: Making up music, words or a dance on the spot, without preparing it in advance.
industrial revolution: The period when factories, machines, steam engines and later electricity changed the way things were made and how people lived.
internet: A huge worldwide network that connects computers and phones, so they can exchange messages, pictures and information.
isolationism: The idea that a country should stay out of the conflicts and affairs of other countries.
jazz: A kind of music born in New Orleans among African Americans, full of rhythm and improvisation. Its instruments include trumpets, saxophones and pianos.
kiva: A round room, partly underground, used by Pueblo peoples for ceremonies and meetings. People entered through a hole in the roof.
light bulb: A glass bulb with a thin wire inside that glows when electricity passes through it, giving light.
lightning rod: A metal rod fixed on top of a building and connected to the ground by a wire, so that lightning passes safely into the earth.
marshal: A federal marshal is a police officer who works for the national government and makes sure court decisions are obeyed.
mass production: Making a very large number of identical objects quickly, with machines and assembly lines, so that they cost less.
microchip: A tiny piece of silicon containing millions of microscopic electronic parts. It is the brain of computers and phones.
mission: A settlement with a church, built by priests to spread Christianity among the local people.
mississippian culture: The civilisation of Native American farmers who lived along the Mississippi River from about 800 to 1600, and built large earth mounds.
mound: A large hill of earth built by hand. Native Americans built mounds as platforms for temples and houses, or as tombs.
nasa: The American space agency, created in 1958. It sends astronauts, rockets and robots into space.
national anthem: The official song of a country, sung at ceremonies and sports events.
national park: A large natural area protected by the government, so that its landscapes, plants and animals are preserved and everyone can visit it.
native american: The Native Americans are the descendants of the first peoples who lived in the Americas long before the Europeans arrived.
neutral: Not taking sides in a war or a disagreement.
nonviolence: Fighting for justice peacefully, without ever using violence, even when you are attacked.
nuclear weapon: A weapon, like an atomic bomb, that uses the energy of atoms and can destroy a whole city.
patent: An official document that proves you invented something and protects your invention, so that others cannot copy it without permission.
pilgrim: The Pilgrims were English Christians who sailed on the Mayflower in 1620 to live their faith freely in America.
pioneer: One of the first people to go and settle in a new place. In America, the pioneers were families who moved west.
plantation: A very large farm, often worked by enslaved people, which grew a single crop to sell, such as tobacco, rice, sugar cane or cotton.
powhatan confederacy: A union of about 30 Native American peoples of Virginia, led by the great chief Powhatan, the father of Pocahontas.
puritan: The Puritans were English Protestants who wanted a simpler, stricter Christian religion, without the ceremonies of the Church of England.
republic: A country where power does not belong to a king but to the people, who elect their leaders for a limited time.
reservation: An area of land set aside by the U.S. government for a Native American nation. Many nations were forced to move onto reservations.
rocket: A vehicle propelled by powerful engines that burn fuel and push gas downwards, strong enough to leave the Earth and go into space.
secession: When a state or region leaves the country it belongs to, to form a separate country.
segregation: Separating people by force because of their skin colour: separate schools, buses, restaurants and neighbourhoods. It was unfair and is now illegal.
separation of powers: The idea that the power to make laws, the power to govern and the power to judge must be held by different people, so that nobody becomes a tyrant.
seven years' war: A war from 1756 to 1763 between Britain and France and their allies, fought in Europe, America, India and on the seas.
share: A small part of a company that people can buy. If the company does well, the share is worth more; if it does badly, it is worth less.
siege: Surrounding a town or a fort with an army to force the people inside to surrender.
slave trade: The capture and sale of people from Africa, who were transported across the Atlantic Ocean in slave ships and sold as slaves in the Americas.
slave trader: A person who bought and sold human beings as slaves.
slavery: A terrible system in which people are treated as property. Enslaved people were bought and sold, forced to work without pay and had no freedom.
soviet union: A large communist country (USSR), from 1922 to 1991, which included Russia and 14 other republics. Its capital was Moscow.
suffrage: The right to vote in elections.
suffragist: A person who campaigned for women's right to vote.
tax: Money that people must pay to the government, so that it can pay for things like roads, schools and the army.
telegraph: A way of sending messages very fast over long distances along electric wires, using a code of short and long signals.
telephone: A device that carries the sound of the voice over long distances, first through wires, today also through radio waves.
terrorist: A person who uses violence and fear against ordinary people to try to force a government to do what they want.
thanksgiving: A national holiday in the United States, on the fourth Thursday of November, when families gather for a big meal to give thanks.
unesco world heritage: A list of the most precious places on Earth, chosen by UNESCO, an organisation of the United Nations, so that they are protected for future generations.
volcano: A mountain or opening in the Earth's crust from which hot melted rock, called lava, ashes and gases can come out.
